title: Review: Natural selection; Stability and change; Climate change

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Biomagnification
items.clue: The increase in the concentration of a persistent toxin in the tissues of organisms at each successive trophic level of a food chain.

items.label: Carrying capacity
items.clue: The maximum population size of a species that a particular environment can sustain over time, set by the limiting resources available.

items.label: Adaptation
items.clue: A heritable characteristic that makes an individual better suited to its environment and so increases its chances of survival and reproduction.

items.label: Tipping point
items.clue: A threshold beyond which a small further change in a variable causes a large, rapid and often irreversible change in the state of an ecosystem.

questions.stem: The replacement of Lamarckism by Darwin's theory of natural selection is described as a paradigm shift. What does the term 'paradigm shift' mean?

options.text: A fundamental change in the framework of ideas within which scientists explain their observations
The first proposal by any scientist that species change over time rather than being fixed
The acceptance that characteristics acquired during life are passed on to offspring
A discovery that proves a scientific theory correct beyond any further doubt

questions.stem: Which statement describes the basis of natural selection due to intraspecific competition?

options.text: Different species compete with one another, and the species that has the best adaptations survives
Individuals improve their adaptations during life, and the improved ones out-compete the rest
Individuals of one species differ in adaptation, so some survive and reproduce more than others
The strongest individuals win fights for resources, and strength is what biologists mean by fitness

questions.stem: What evidence indicates that an ecosystem has persisted, and so shown stability, for millions of years?

options.text: Fossil pollen from dated layers of sediment shows the same type of plant community persisting through geological time.
The oldest individual trees now growing in the ecosystem have been dated at several thousand years old.
Census data show that the population size of every species has stayed exactly constant from year to year.
The ecosystem has a high rate of primary production and supports a very large number of species.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions is required for an ecosystem to remain stable?

options.text: Recycling of both energy and nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, large population sizes and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables that are held perfectly constant.

questions.stem: In 1970 the area of a rainforest was 4 000 000 km². By 2020 the area was 3 320 000 km². What is the percentage change in the area of forest?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100 = (3 320 000 − 4 000 000) ÷ 4 000 000 × 100 = −680 000 ÷ 4 000 000 × 100 = −17.0%. The negative sign shows a decrease from the original area of forest.

questions.stem: Which practice increases the sustainability of agriculture on a farm?

options.text: Applying extra inorganic fertilizer every year so that all the nutrients lost by leaching are replaced.
Growing cover crops between harvests so that the soil is protected from erosion and less nitrate is leached away.
Ploughing sloping fields deeply each year, because soil is replaced by weathering as fast as it is lost.
Replacing manure with manufactured nitrogen fertilizer, since the fertilizer adds nothing to the farm's carbon footprint.

questions.stem: Why does mercury released from industry reach high concentrations in large predatory fish such as tuna?

options.text: Large fish swallow the greatest volume of water while feeding, so they take in more mercury than smaller fish do.
Mercury taken in with prey is retained in tissues rather than excreted, so its concentration rises at each trophic level up to the tuna.
Tuna swim through polluted water for years and absorb mercury through their gills rather than from their food.
Tuna live for many years, so they accumulate mercury over time; smaller fish would reach the same level if they lived as long.

questions.stem: Which statement about plastic pollution of the oceans is correct?

options.text: Marine bacteria biodegrade plastics, but so slowly that the material persists for a few decades before disappearing.
Microplastics are too small to harm marine animals, so only macroplastics have effects on marine life.
Macroplastics fragment into microplastics but are not broken down by decomposers, so the material persists.
Microplastics enter the oceans only as manufactured particles such as microbeads, not from larger plastic items.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the approach used to restore native forest at Hinewai Reserve in New Zealand?

options.text: Grazing livestock were removed and introduced gorse was left as a nurse canopy, under which native trees regenerated with minimal interference.
Native tree seedlings were raised in nurseries and planted across the whole reserve in place of the former pasture and scrub.
The introduced gorse was cleared with herbicide and machinery before native forest was allowed to return to the area.
Native forest was allowed to recover in scattered small patches across the peninsula, since connecting habitats over one large area is not needed.

questions.stem: Which is an anthropogenic cause of the rise in the atmospheric concentration of methane since pre-industrial times?

options.text: Exhalation of waste gases by the greatly increased human population
Enteric fermentation in the growing numbers of ruminant farm livestock
Complete combustion of coal and petroleum in vehicles and power stations
Escape of ancient methane trapped in bubbles in melting polar ice

questions.explanation: Methanogenic archaea in the guts of cattle and other ruminants release methane, and livestock numbers have risen greatly. Rice paddies, landfill and leakage from fossil fuel extraction are other anthropogenic sources.

questions.stem: Which process is part of a positive feedback cycle that increases global warming?

options.text: More evaporation forms clouds that reflect sunlight and cool the surface
Melting snow and ice absorb heat from their surroundings and cool the oceans
Warming ocean water dissolves more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
Thawing permafrost releases methane gas into the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Methane is released from melting permafrost as previously frozen organic matter decomposes anaerobically. Methane is a greenhouse gas, so this causes further warming and further thawing: a positive feedback cycle.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches a threat to coral reefs with its cause?

options.text: Coral bleaching is caused by ocean acidification, which dissolves the pigments out of the coral tissue.
Suppression of calcification in corals is caused by the increased carbon dioxide concentration of seawater.
Ocean acidification lowers the pH of seawater below 7, so the calcium carbonate skeletons of corals dissolve away.
Coral bleaching kills the polyps immediately, so a reef that has bleached can no longer recover.
